title: Span and Memory
summary: Look at part of an array or string without copying it, and learn why that makes code fast.

steps.title: Allocations are not free
body: A quick recap. Local variables of value types live on the **stack**: claiming and releasing that space costs almost nothing. Objects, arrays and strings live on the **heap**: each one is an **allocation**, and the garbage collector must later find it and clean it up.
One allocation is cheap. A million are not. And some everyday methods allocate more than you might think:
```csharp
string line = "2024-11-24";
string year = line.Substring(0, 4);     // a NEW string: 4 characters copied to the heap
string[] parts = line.Split('-');       // a new array AND three new strings
Strings cannot change, so `Substring` has no choice but to copy. To read four characters you paid for a whole new object.
Code that parses a large file line by line can spend most of its time creating and collecting little strings like these. The tools in this lesson exist to avoid that.

options: It allocates a new string on the heap and copies four characters into it
It returns a view of the first four characters of `line`, without copying
It shortens `line` itself to four characters
It stores four characters on the stack
steps.explain: Strings are immutable and every string is its own heap object, so a substring is always a copy.

steps.title: Span<T>: a window, not a copy
body: A `Span<T>` is a **view** over memory that already exists. It is tiny: it only remembers where to start and how many items it covers. Creating one allocates nothing.
```csharp
Span<int> all = temps.AsSpan();
Span<int> middle = temps.AsSpan(1, 3);    // start at index 1, length 3: 21, 25, 19
Span<int> last2 = all.Slice(3);           // from index 3 to the end: 19, 16
Span<int> same = all[3..];                // range syntax works too
Because a span is a window onto the original, **writing through it changes the array**:
```csharp
middle[0] = 99;
Console.WriteLine(temps[1]);    // 99
For strings, which must never change, there is `ReadOnlySpan<char>`:
```csharp
ReadOnlySpan<char> year = "2024-11-24".AsSpan(0, 4);    // no copy, no allocation
A span has `Length`, an indexer, `foreach`, `IndexOf`, `Slice` and more, so it feels much like an array.

steps.explain: `middle` covers indexes 1 to 3 of the array. Its item 0 *is* the array's item 1, so the write shows through. Its last item is the array's item 3.

steps.prompt: Read the year out of the date without allocating a new string.
steps.explain: `AsSpan` views the string, `Slice` narrows the view, and `int.Parse` has an overload that reads straight from a `ReadOnlySpan<char>`.

steps.title: Sum without Split
prompt: Write `static int SumCsv(ReadOnlySpan<char> text)` that adds up comma-separated whole numbers **without creating any strings**.
Useful span members: `IndexOf(',')` (returns -1 when there is none), `Slice(start)`, `Slice(start, length)`, and `int.Parse(span)`.
starter: // TODO: while there is text left, find the next comma,
//       parse what is before it, and move past it
template: Dojo.Eq("It works on a slice of a longer string", 6, SumCsv("total=1,2,3;".AsSpan(6, 5)));

forbid.message: Creates no strings or arrays: no Split, Substring, ToString or ToArray

hints: You may reassign the parameter: `text = text.Slice(comma + 1);` moves the window past the comma.
Inside a `while (text.Length > 0)` loop: `int comma = text.IndexOf(',');`. If it is -1, the rest of the text is the last number.

steps.title: stackalloc: scratch space on the stack
body: Sometimes you need a small temporary buffer. `new int[8]` would put it on the heap. `stackalloc` puts it on the stack instead, and a span lets you use it safely:
```csharp
Span<int> digits = stackalloc int[8];
digits[0] = 4;
digits[1] = 2;
There is no allocation and nothing for the garbage collector to do. The buffer simply disappears when the method returns.
Two rules keep this safe:
- **Keep it small.** The stack is limited to about a megabyte. A few hundred bytes is fine; a size that comes from user input is not.
- **It cannot outlive the method.** You cannot return it or store it anywhere.

steps.explain: The buffer holds 0, 1, 4, 9. The slice from index 2 covers 4 and 9, which add up to 13.

steps.title: The rules of Span, and Memory<T>
body: A span may point at the stack, so the compiler makes sure a span itself **never leaves the stack**. `Span<T>` is a special kind of struct (a `ref struct`), and that brings restrictions:
- it cannot be a **field of a class**
- it cannot be used **across an `await`** (the method's variables move to the heap while it waits)
- it cannot be **captured by a lambda** or put in a `List<Span<T>>`
Spans are for *here and now*: locals and parameters in ordinary methods.

When you need to **hold on** to a piece of an array, in a field or across an `await`, use `Memory<T>`. It is an ordinary struct that can live anywhere. When it is time to do the actual work, ask it for a span:
```csharp
class Packet
private readonly Memory<byte> _payload;          // fine as a field
public Packet(Memory<byte> payload) => _payload = payload;
public int Checksum()
Span<byte> bytes = _payload.Span;            // a span, just for this method
int sum = 0;
foreach (byte b in bytes) sum += b;
return sum;

items: A `Span<int>` local variable in an ordinary method
A `Span<byte>` local used both before and after an `await`
A lambda that captures a `Span<int>` local
steps.explain: Everything in the error bucket would move a span off the stack and onto the heap. `Memory<T>` is the type built for those places.

steps.prompt: Match each tool to what it gives you.
pairs: a view over the whole array, with no copy
a narrower view of the same memory
a small buffer that vanishes when the method returns
a view that may be stored in a field or kept across an `await`
a new heap array holding a copy

steps.title: Parse 09:00-10:30 without allocating
prompt: **Sidekick piece: `sk log 3 09:00-10:30`.** Log time by hand, and import long time-tracker exports without creating thousands of throwaway strings.

1. `static bool TryParseClock(ReadOnlySpan<char> text, out TimeOnly time)`: trim the span; it must be `H:MM` or `HH:MM` (one or two digits, a colon, exactly two digits) with hour 0..23 and minute 0..59. On success `time` is that time.
2. `static bool TryParseRange(ReadOnlySpan<char> text, out TimeOnly start, out TimeOnly end)`: `start-end` split at the first `-`; both sides must parse and `end` must be later than `start`.
TryParseRange("09:00-10:30", out var a, out var b)   // true, 09:00 and 10:30
Use slices (`text[..colon]`) and `int.TryParse` on spans: no `Split`, no `Substring`. Like `TryParseMinutes` from Methods and collections, a `Try...` method never throws on bad input.
starter: static bool TryParseClock(ReadOnlySpan<char> text, out TimeOnly time)
static bool TryParseRange(ReadOnlySpan<char> text, out TimeOnly start, out TimeOnly end)
solution: static bool TryParseClock(ReadOnlySpan<char> text, out TimeOnly time)
if (colon < 1 || colon > 2 || text.Length - colon - 1 != 2) return false;
if (!int.TryParse(text[..colon], out int hours) || !int.TryParse(text[(colon + 1)..], out int minutes)) return false;
if (hours is < 0 or > 23 || minutes is < 0 or > 59) return false;
static bool TryParseRange(ReadOnlySpan<char> text, out TimeOnly start, out TimeOnly end)
return TryParseClock(text[..dash], out start) && TryParseClock(text[(dash + 1)..], out end) && end > start;
template: string DojoP(string s) => TryParseClock(s, out var t) ? t.ToString("HH:mm") : "false";
Dojo.Eq("a slice of a longer command", "10:30", TryParseClock("log 3 10:30-11:00".AsSpan(6, 5), out var dojoSlice) ? dojoSlice.ToString("HH:mm") : "false");
Dojo.Eq("24:00 is not a time", "false", DojoP("24:00"));
Dojo.Eq("12:60 is not a time", "false", DojoP("12:60"));
string DojoR(string s) => TryParseRange(s, out var a, out var b) ? $"{a:HH:mm}-{b:HH:mm}" : "false";
Dojo.Eq("a range that ends before it starts", "false", DojoR("10:30-09:00"));

forbid.message: Works on slices, without Split, Substring or new strings

hints: `text = text.Trim(); int colon = text.IndexOf(':');` then `if (colon < 1 || colon > 2 || text.Length - colon - 1 != 2) return false;`.
`int.TryParse(text[..colon], out int hours)` and `int.TryParse(text[(colon + 1)..], out int minutes)`, then check the ranges and `time = new TimeOnly(hours, minutes);`.
`TryParseRange`: find the `-`, then `TryParseClock(text[..dash], out start) && TryParseClock(text[(dash + 1)..], out end) && end > start`. Assign `end = default;` first so every path sets it.
